title: Sell Mineral Rights in Converse County, WY
metaTitle: Sell Mineral Rights in Converse County, WY
metaDescription: Own mineral rights in Converse County, WY? Douglas and Glenrock sit inside one of Wyoming's most active stacked-lateral horizontal oil plays. Get a real read.
heroLead: Converse County has been ground zero for one of Wyoming's most active horizontal drilling booms of the past decade, and if you're holding a mineral interest around Douglas or Glenrock, there's a real chance it's tied to genuinely current production.
intro: Operators including Devon Energy, Chesapeake, Continental Resources, and others have drilled dense multi-well pads targeting stacked pay zones here, the Niobrara, Turner, and Sussex formations chief among them, often from a single surface location with laterals reaching out in multiple directions to drain different intervals at different depths. This kind of stacked-lateral development has made Converse County one of the more actively drilled counties in the state through much of the 2010s and into the 2020s.

That density changes what I need from you before pricing an interest. Because so many wells here were drilled recently, with modern completion techniques, decline curves and unit configurations vary a lot even within a few miles, and I lean heavily on your actual trailing royalty statements rather than county-wide assumptions.

sections.heading: Stacked pay and horizontal density
paragraphs: Where an older Wyoming field might have one productive zone, Converse County's newer development often targets three or four stacked intervals from the same well pad. That means a single spacing unit can have multiple horizontal wellbores contributing to your royalty check, which is part of why interests here can carry meaningfully more current income than comparable acreage in a single-zone field elsewhere in the state.
It also means unitization and pooling paperwork around here tends to be more complex than older, simpler conventional leases. I take the time to read through it rather than skip to a number.

sections.heading: Douglas and Glenrock as development hubs
paragraphs: Douglas, the county seat, and Glenrock to the west have both served as staging points for drilling activity that's radiated out across the county over the past decade. Courthouse records in Douglas reflect that pace, with lease filings, unit agreements, and division orders processed at a volume this county hadn't seen since much older conventional development decades earlier.
If your family's interest sits inside one of these newer horizontal units, your production history is probably recent enough that I can price it with real precision rather than broad estimates.

sections.heading: Commodity exposure and decline behavior
paragraphs: Horizontal wells in this play show the classic pattern, strong initial production followed by a steep decline in the first year or two, then a longer, shallower tail. Where your specific wells sit on that curve, combined with current oil price levels, drives most of what your interest is worth today. I never quote a flat number without seeing your actual statements first, because this play moves too much with the market for that to be honest.

sections.heading: What I check before I quote
paragraphs: Converse County recorder records for your chain of title, current well and unit status through the Wyoming Oil and Gas Conservation Commission, and your trailing royalty history if you have it. That combination tells me whether we're pricing an active, multi-well producing interest or acreage on the fringe of the play that hasn't seen a permit yet.

sections.heading: Older conventional history beneath the new plays
paragraphs: Before the current stacked-lateral boom, Converse County had a longer, quieter history of conventional production in various pockets around the county, wells that predate horizontal drilling entirely. Some mineral interests here carry that older lease and royalty history layered underneath the newer horizontal activity, which matters when I'm reconstructing a complete title and production picture for an owner.
I check both eras separately, since an interest with decades of conventional history plus recent horizontal activity tells a very different story than one that's purely new.

Glenrock in particular has a longer conventional oil history than a lot of people realize, tied to smaller fields that produced steadily for decades before the current stacked-lateral boom ever arrived. If your family's interest traces to that earlier era, I want to see whatever old royalty statements or lease documents still exist, since they establish a baseline production history worth factoring into today's number.

faqs.question: Is Converse County still being actively drilled?
faqs.answer: Yes, in significant parts of the county, though pace shifts with commodity prices. I'll check current activity near your specific tract.

faqs.question: What does stacked-lateral development mean for my royalty?
faqs.answer: It can mean multiple horizontal wells across different formations contribute to the same spacing unit, potentially increasing your income compared to a single-zone field.

faqs.question: My royalty checks are recent and growing. Should I still consider selling?
faqs.answer: Possibly, depending on your goals and where the underlying wells sit on their decline curve. I'll walk you through the actual numbers before recommending anything.

faqs.question: How do you price something this recently developed?
faqs.answer: Primarily from your actual trailing royalty statements and current well status, rather than broad county averages, since recent horizontal plays vary significantly section to section.

faqs.question: Are Douglas and Glenrock in the same play?
faqs.answer: Both sit within the broader stacked-lateral development trend, though specific well density and formation targets vary. I'll check your exact location.

faqs.question: What if my interest has no production history at all?
faqs.answer: I'll price it as undeveloped acreage tied to the broader stacked-lateral trend, distinct from an active producing unit, and explain the difference clearly.
